name: King and pawn endgames
goal: You can tell whether king and pawn win against a lone king, using the opposition and the key squares in front of the pawn.
intro: Two ideas decide most endgames with only kings and pawns: the rule of the square, which tells you whether a king can catch a pawn, and the opposition, the stand-off between two kings with one square between them. A passed pawn far from the other pawns, an outside passed pawn, is often enough to win.

parts.title: The rule of the square
parts.text: Draw a square from the pawn to its queening square (e5-e8-b8-b5). If the enemy king can step into it, it catches the pawn; if not, the pawn queens. Black's king on a4 is outside the square.

notes.text: With White to move the black king is outside the square, so just push.
The pawn queens. Had Black been to move, 1...Kb5 would have stepped into the square and caught it.

parts.title: The opposition
parts.text: The kings face each other with one square between them and it is Black to move, so you have the opposition: Black has to give way.
parts.line: Kd6 Kf5 Kd7 Kf6 Kd6 e4 Kd7 e5 Ke8 Ke6 Kd8 Kf7 Kd7 e6+ Kd6 e7

notes.text: Black's king stepped aside, so yours goes forward.
Black seems to have the opposition now, but you don't have to move your king: a pawn move hands the move back to Black.
Your king stands in front of the pawn on the sixth rank, and the pawn will get through.

parts.title: The outside passed pawn
parts.text: Pawns are equal, but your f-pawn is far from the others. Use it as a decoy.
parts.line: f5 Kd6 f6 Ke6 Kxc5 Kxf6 Kb6 Ke6 Kxa6 Kd7 Kb7

notes.text: Push the outside pawn so the black king has to chase it.
While Black's king is away, yours eats the queenside pawns.
Your king shields the a-pawn, and it will queen.
